utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless the Court has procedural matters it wishes to raise, we're prepared with the next witness, and it will be handled by Mr. Colin Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. We don't have anything. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps before the witness is brought in, I would just say that, in light of your comments on the first day back, which I guess was last Monday, we have drastically reduced the number of documents that we intended to admit through this witness. I would say it's less than one-third of the ones cited in this report as we'd originally planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, can I interrupt you. You're not coming through. I'm not quite sure if I heard what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me try to speak a little closer to the microphone, Your Honour. I was just saying that in light of the Chamber's comments a week ago, we have drastically reduced the number of exhibits that we intend to tender through this witness. It's less than a third, certainly, than what we had previously intended. We will not seek the admission of any documents from the first two sections of his report and will focus just on the last two sections on the most important documents therein. I hope that meets with the Chamber's approval. I would say in relation to those documents that a number of them deal specifically with the accused, and many, if not all of them are documents from the relevant time period. They're military orders, reports, decisions. These kind of contemporaneous documents that have real evidentiary value in themselves rather than reports looking back on things that were done before. So I would also say, Your Honour, that most of the documents are very short. There are some longer ones, and when that's the case, we will make an effort to identify the specific pages and passages that are most important for the Chamber's attention. I hope that meets with Your Honours' approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Black, I think you may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would call the next Prosecution witness, Mr. Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens. Can you hear me okay? The first thing, I would like you to please read the solemn declaration, which will be handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The microphones need to be turned on. You may have to repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, if you can come a little closer to your mike. You just don't come through on my mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Black:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I believe you may be seated. Mr. Theunens, I know you've testified before - this is something that I forget myself - because we're both speaking in English, out of consideration for the interpreters we both need to speak slowly. And in addition to that, if you could try to leave a pause between my question and your answer, I'll try to do the same between your questions -- between, excuse me, your answers and my questions, and in that way we'll give them time to keep up. Also, if at any time you don't understand one of my questions, please just tell me and I'll try to state it more clearly. The first topic will just be some personal background information on your professional experience. Please state your full name and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: My full name is Reynaud Theunens, and I'm from Belgian nationality, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could, please briefly describe your military experience prior to joining the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I went to military academy in Belgium in 1983. I ended my studies there at the end of 1987 when I went for six months to armoured school. After that I was doing three years posted in an armoured battalion in Germany, part of the Belgian armed forces in Germany, where I carried out the duties of first platoon commander and then personnel officer. After that, I returned for one year to the military academy to be what we call a promotion commander. It's an instructor who is responsible for first years. First I was a deputy promotion commander, then a promotion commander. After that, and that was in September 1992, I joined, or I was called to join the Belgium military intelligence security service, where I became a Balkans intelligence analyst, and basically I carried out that duty until May 2000 where I received another assignment within the Belgium Military Intelligence Service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you did mention this by implication, but so it's clear, where were you working in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In May 1995, I was part of the UNPF - United Nations Peace Forces - headquarters in Zagreb, where I worked as a military information officer. I joined -- or I was sent by Belgium to work at UNPROFOR, was the name then, in December 1994, and I took up an assignment at the headquarters of military information officer, which I kept until October 1995, and later on I also joined other peace -- or participated in other peace operations in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And briefly, at that time you were in Zagreb, what were your duties? Just summarise.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: When I arrived, Your Honours, I was responsible for -- responsible to keep orders of battle, to keep structures of the parties in Croatia, both Croatian armed forces as well as the armed forces of the entity that was known as Republika Serbian Krajina, but due to the fact that I had previous experience working on the Balkans, I received another assignment and I became part of what was called the assessment desk. My duties there consisted -- together with a Swedish colleague. My duties consisted of reviewing the operational information we received from battalions on the field and to try to assess the implications of these developments, of the developments described in that information. So I had to draft written reports for the headquarters, for the force commander, the chief of staff, and other military officials. Together with my Swedish colleague, we were also involved in preparing and giving briefings for force commander as well as on requirement for Mr. Akashi, who was the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, and there were also other activities related to -- to that work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient for the time. When did you begin your current employment at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I started to work for the ICTY on the 28th of June, 2001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are currently an intelligence analyst in the military analysis team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the military analysis team; could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The military analysis team is a team within the Office of the Prosecutor, and consisting of people with a military background, most of us have also intelligence background and have spent time in the former Yugoslavia. Our duties consist, generally speaking, of providing what I would call military support to investigations and prosecutions. This military support is focused on what I would call both technical as well as doctrinal issues. For example, we can provide -- we will review information and analyse information on technical capabilities of weapons systems. We will also look at structures, try to identify --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We will look at, analyse structures of armed forces as well as the organisation, look at doctrinal aspects, and that mainly focused on the issue of command and control both within the military as well as between the military and the political authorities. And I want to emphasise that this doesn't only include de jure aspects but also de facto aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can go slowly, Mr. Theunens. You heard the interpreter asking if you could slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will be something that we'll both have to work on. I'll try to help you remember and help myself remember. Mr. Theunens, is the military analysis team part of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does that affect your analysis, if at all, either in the analytical process that you use or in the reports that you prepare?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I received the assignment, the task for this report from Senior Trial Attorney Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and it's obvious that most of the information, or the information I used to compile this report was accessible through the evidence that is available at the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, I want to emphasise that there is a huge amount of documentary as well as other evidence available and this evidence consists all aspects of the conflict; it's not particularly directed against one party or in favour of another party. So when I compare it to the information I had access to both during my studies when, for example, preparing a dissertation or when working as an intelligence analyst in Belgium, I think that here I have access to a much wider range of sources, in particular what I would call primary sources. We have original military documents, we have original doctrinal documents. We don't have to rely, for example -- I didn't rely for this report on, for example, statements of people who had seen something or heard something, which are then actually secondary sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll turn in a moment to the -- to the process, the analytical process, but let me ask you, since you've been with the military analysis team, which is also called the MAT, or the M-A-T, have you specialised or focused on any particular area or areas?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've mainly been working on cases that involve Serb perpetrators in Croatia. So I testified in the Milosevic case based on a report I prepared on the role of the SFRY armed forces in the conflict in Croatia. I've compiled a similar report for the Vukovar case, where I plan to testify later this year; and I'm preparing a report for the Seselj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Theunens' CV was filed on the 25th of February in connection the submission of his expert report, and it bears the ERN 04668426 to 8427. If that could be pulled up on the E-court, I'd like to offer it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on the screen in front of you I hope you'll see a document. Is that your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's the first page of the curriculum vitae, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no objections to exhibiting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What exhibit number will it be given?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 20, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit number 20. Thank you very much. Proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you've referred to a report which you prepared for this case. Do you have a copy of that report before you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have a copy of the report in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read to me the title of that report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The title of the report is "Military Analysis Team expert report, case IT-95-11-T, Milan Martic and the SAO Krajina/RSK TO-SVK." And then I have different parts of it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report was admitted by your written decision of the 13th of January of this year, and it has been assigned Exhibit Number 6. I don't know if you have your copies with you, so I brought copies in English and in B/C/S, for the Defence. I think it's going to be necessary to have a hard copy, because as we go through the report, we'll also be pulling documents up on E-court. So rather than having the court officer flip between pages of the report and documents, if we can all follow along in the hard copy, that would be the easiest course, I believe. Your Honours, while we're in the process of passing this out, I've also printed out colour pages of specific pages of the report because the maps and other graphs that are included in the report, at least in my photocopied version, were not legible. So I have for everyone colour copies to make it easier to see those graphs and maps. With the assistance of the usher, I'll pass those out at this time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My thanks to the usher for helping out with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, have you had an opportunity to review your report since it was filed in February of 2005?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, indeed I had the opportunity to review my report and I noticed there were some typographic and similar errors in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you produce a corrigendum to the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, a corrigendum was produced, both covering errors in the footnotes where we, for one or the other reason, the erroneous 65 ter numbers were used, and then there are also some minor adjustments to the contents of the report in the second part of the corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask, with the assistance of the court officers, if we could pull this document up on the E-court. The ERN is 04668250 to 8251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While that document is being pulled up, Mr. Black, the Chamber is aware that in the last couple of minutes you've handed up quite a voluminous amount of documentation. We have to devise ways of making sure that it's tendered into evidence properly and it's given correct exhibit numbers. I don't know whether at this stage you don't want to propose tendering in the report, at least, before we come to the documents, which I would suggest that, when they come, they come as the A, B, C, D of the number of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the most part I'm going to try to do everything electronically. It's a bit of test run with E-court. So far what we've handed up is the report which was already admitted into evidence by a written decision earlier this year. So what was handed up is Exhibit 6. I am sorry if that was confusing. The particular pages are just printouts in colour pages of the particular pages of that report, so it's also part of Exhibit 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if you could have a look at the screen in front of you. Do you recognise what's there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. In this case that is the first page of the corrigendum, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that also be -- could this also be made an exhibit so we have a record of the changes to the report, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit Number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you mentioned earlier that you were asked by the prior Senior Trial Attorney to prepare a report for this case. What precisely were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was asked to prepare what is called an expert report on the SAO -- on structures known as the SAO Krajina and later RSK TO, Territorial Defence, and the SVK, SVK being the acronym for the Serbian army of the Serbian Krajina, and on the relation between these armed structures and Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you a couple of questions about the scope of your report. First, what was the main focus of your analysis? Perhaps it's clear from the title but if you could just state that, please, the main focus.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Actually, the main focus was included in the answer of the previous question. So the focus was actually to try to first of all describe these structures. I knew from the Milosevic case and the work done there what Territorial Defence was. In this particular report the focus was then on the Territorial Defence as it was established in the entity known as the SAO, the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina. And also later when this SAO Krajina was transformed into the RSK, and also -- so you look at the structure, you analyse that, you look at the activities of those structures, their role in relation to the indictment. And more importantly then was to try to find out and try to establish the link, the relationship between the person of Milan Martic and these armed structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to look into any crimes committed -- or excuse me. Did you look at the structure or organisation of any Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I didn't look at the structure of any Croatian armed forces in detail. Obviously when reviewing documents I used for this report, I came across information that dealt with the structure of Croatian armed forces, but that's not part of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to look into crimes allegedly committed by Croatian forces or who might have been responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I would give the same reply, Your Honours. Obviously when first of all trying to identify information that I could use for this report, and also reviewing that information, I came across information that dealt with crimes allegedly committed by Croatian forces, but that information was not included in this report as it is outside the scope of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your report address the organisation or structure of the Serb police forces in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I'm aware that there will also be a witness who will specifically talk about what we MUP, or Ministry of Interior forces; i.e., police. And again some passages of my report may mention police forces of the SAO Krajina and RSK, but they were not part of the focus of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving from scope to sources, what kinds of sources did you rely on in preparing the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Basically the sources can be divided in four categories. First of all there are what I would call legal documents. Even though I'm not a legal expert or legal analyst, I thought it would be useful to include the basic aspects of the laws that existed both in the SFRY as well as in the entities known as SAO Krajina, and later RSK, into the report, and I mean by that aspects of the law that address command and control and duties and structure of armed forces. So that would be the first category. The second category, military documents. These military documents cover doctrine as it existed in the JNA as well as in the SAO Krajina, RSK, TO, and SVK. The structure, duties and so on, as well as orders and reports. A third category are documents that were compiled by the UN peace forces; and a fourth group would consist of open source, and that refers to newspaper articles even though I tried to be very restrictive in the use of newspaper articles. And actually there was not a need to use many open sources because we have so many what I would call primary military documents which actually cover the requirements of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned military documents. Could you please be more specific about what kinds or from where they came. Who originated the military documents that you used?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The military documents, Your Honours, could be divided in, let's say, two groups of documents. First of all, there are like manuals and regulations that deal with structure, doctrine, organisation. There is, for example, also a JNA regulation on how the SFRY armed forces, JNA and TO were to implement international laws of armed conflict. In addition to that, there are also orders, which can be one-page documents, and for more complicated issues we would have a 15-page order, as well as reports. Reporting is one of the essential functions for militaries, for military forces to be able to operate; i.e., the command has at all times to be aware of what is happening not only in the units subordinated to him but also he has to know what his superior command is doing, and this information is -- can be forward or transmitted via reports, and some of these reports are included in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question on that. Are these Croatian military documents or documents from the Serb entities that you'll talk about, or from where did they come?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The military documents I used originated from the JNA, so the Yugoslav People's Army as it existed until May 1992; the VJ, so the successor structure to the JNA - VJ, Vojska Jugoslavija - as well as the SAO Krajina/RSK Territorial Defence, and the SVK. These documents originate from various sources. I can say that most of the documents were obtained from the Croatian authorities. In particular in 1995 during the Operation Flash in Western Slavonia, the first -- that started on 1st of May, and subsequently the Operation Storm, which started on the 4th of August 1995. The Croatian forces managed to seize enormous quantities of documents of the RSK and SVK. These documents were then stored in archives in Croatia and staff of the OTP was granted access to these archives. I, for example, even though it's a bit outside of my framework of my professional activities, I participated twice in such an archives mission where the staff of the OTP visits archives. I went once to Zagreb, another to Petrinja, having the opportunity to review documents. And we also collected documents there which were then introduced in the system here and also used for my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your work have you developed or formed any views about the authenticity of these documents or certain categories of these documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Of course, it would be -- as -- when you look -- when you see all these documents and you seem the quantity of the documents and also the contents of the documents, one concern is, of course, authenticity. Now there are various ways to do that. One thing we did, for example, was to compare those documents with documents we had already in-house obtained from other sources, and it could be there are examples where similar orders have been obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from different sources. For example, an order from the VJ to the SVK, we will probably find in the Croatian archives the copy the SVK received. Now, in some cases we asked Serbia and Montenegro for the initial order, the VJ order, and when we obtained it, we can compare both orders. We can do that based on the reference number. What we also did was to show documents to witnesses we interviewed. For example, a number of senior officers of the SVK, so the armed forces of the entity known as the RSK. During these interviews we showed them documents we had seized or we had obtained via archives in Croatia, and we asked these witness whether they could authenticate these documents. A number of documents were also used in my report for the Milosevic case, and I assume that there the Defence had a look at the documents, because of course they were disclosed, and again witnesses who testified in that trial also had an opportunity to look at these reports -- to these documents, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you touched on the analytical process you used and now you've described the sources that were available. In just a few sentences could you explain the process by which you take those sources and turn them into a report such as you prepared for this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Intelligence work is generally done according to a process which is called the intelligence cycle. The intelligence cycle consists of four phases. The first phase is called direction. In this case I received a direction from the senior trial attorney who asked me to prepare a report on the topics I mentioned earlier; SAO, RSK, TO, and SVK and the relationship between Milan Martic and these armed structures. Based on direction, the second phase will be launched, and that phase is called collection. Collection means that you are going to look for information that is required in order to fulfil the demands expressed in the direction. So what I did, as an analyst I consulted the various databases that are available in the OTP to look for documents that, in my view, were useful for this report. It's obvious that during that process there would also be Rule 68 material, for example, that would be discovered and disclosed in accordance with the appropriate procedures. The next step is the processing phase, and actually analysis is part of the processing phase. Basically - and I will try to put it in very short sentence - you try -- you're going to identify information that you may -- that you consider useful for further use as an analyst in a sense that the processing consists of four steps. First of all, your collation. It means that you're going to organise your information. That's not so important. Then, more importantly, you're going to evaluate the information. That consists of two aspects: Looking -- that means -- it implies assessing the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information, which are two different things. After that, once you have decided that -- determined that the information is credible and it's a reliable source, you will analyse it; i.e., you will review it and determine elements in that information that are relevant for further interpretation. Interpretation then means that you're going to compare the new information with what you already know in order to identify relevant facts - a practical example here - what I would include in the report. And then lastly, when I go back to the intelligence cycle, the fourth -- the fourth phase of the intelligence cycle is called dissemination; i.e., the distribution of the information - of the intelligence, actually - the intelligence to those that have an interest in obtaining it, and that was then done via this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. We've talked about your background now and the process and the sources. Soon I'm going to ask you about the substance of the report but there are just two more preliminary matters. The first one, if I could ask, with the assistance of the case manager and the usher again, we're going to pass out the maps booklet. As you will recall, we raised this issue before. The Chamber asked the parties to meet and discuss the maps booklet and try to reach agreement. We have had some letters back and forth, and I think -- I don't want to speak for the Defence, but I think we've agreed now. We made a number of changes based on their comments, so I think now we're ready to offer these map booklets into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been done in several cases, including the last trial I worked on, and I think it was helpful to both parties and to the Chamber. Also, a couple of these maps, in particular map 1 and map 7, are already in evidence because they are associated with some of the 92 bis evidence that was admitted by Your Honours. If the Chamber likes, I can take the witness through each map and ask him a couple questions, but the procedure in other cases has been simply to admit this map booklet and then different witnesses can refer to it during the entire trial. Mr. Theunens will refer it to it once or twice. Not to all of the maps but some of them, and other witnesses continuing with the trial can use this and it is a reference that everyone has handy. So I would move this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you say that Mr. Theunens is also going to use the maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, he will, Your Honour. He will refer to one or two of the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 22, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the map is -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. One somewhat related matter, and for this I would ask again -- I think it is a last hard copy item for the day -- with the assistance of the usher and Ms. Walpita, if I could distribute -- this is an atlas that has been obviously disclosed to the Defence. If the witness could have a copy and four copies for Your Honours, as well as one copy for the registry. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it one copy for --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: For the registry, Your Honour. Please correct me if that's not the right procedure, but I think the Chamber has requested four copies of most hard copy documents, one for the witness to look at, although that may then become the exhibit for the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honour. And I think we may have an extra copy for them if they don't have it here today, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. This atlas, Concise Atlas of the Republic of Croatia and of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, can we give it an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would just make clear that we offer this as a reference for the parties and the Trial Chamber as to the maps. There's also a copy of census data from 1991 in the back, but there's a text talking about history and the Croatian coat of arms and things like that. We don't intend to rely on that evidence. It's for the maps and, to a limited extent, that census data in the back. Just so that's clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get assistance? Usually, even when you speak in English, I can hear you on my earphones here. I've not been able to hear you at all today, and you speak a little softly for me. I'm a bit hard of hearing. I do rely on this to hear. If somebody can help me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I've tried to take whatever steps I can on my end, and hopefully that's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've taken steps on my end. Now I've become a technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting reminds me to ask -- or mention to the Chamber that we don't have any extra copies of this atlas. It's a little bit more expensive than most of the things we have, so we just have a limited copy. Just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can put that atlas aside, Mr. Theunens. Thank you. Turning now to the report itself. The first thing, before we dive in, I'd like you to turn to the table of contents, and maybe the Chamber could follow along here. Just a quick word as to format as we do that. After the Table of Contents, and there is an Overview and Executive Summary, then the report has four sections. Within each section is a brief summary which is then followed by the full analysis, and I would note that there's a very helpful glossary at the end of the report. That contains a whole list of abbreviations that are used not only by Mr. Theunens in the report but I am sure they will be used by other witnesses as trial goes on. I find it very useful. You might also have occasion to look at it. So everyone has an idea where we're going, we'll cover section 1 first, which is important background information. I won't ask to admit any of the exhibits there, any of the documents. Not because they're not important, of course, but because I understand from Your Honours that we need to get through this. I'll mostly skip over section 2, and then we'll focus on sections 3 and 4, which are the core of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you -- now I have too much of this. But didn't you say that the report has already been admitted as Exhibit 6? So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I apologise for the confusion. The report is in evidence. The report, of course, refers to and relies on a number of documents. I will seek to admit into evidence several of those documents but only from sections 3 and 4; nothing from section 1 or 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we'll begin with section 1, which starts on page 2 of the report, which is page 20 in the B/C/S translation. I don't know if Defence is using the B/C/S version. Because of the translation there is quite a discrepancy in the pages. I will make an effort every time I mention a page number to also give the page in the B/C/S version to try to keep everyone on track. In fact, Mr. Theunens, if you could please go ahead and turn to pages 4 and 5 of your report, which is page 23 of the B/C/S. What were the constituent parts of the SFRY armed forces? And when I say "SFRY," that's an abbreviation for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the SFRY armed forces consisted of the JNA and the TO, the JNA being the Yugoslav People's Army - sometimes translated as National, so Yugoslav National Army - and the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look, then, at pages 5 to 6 of your report, pages 23 to 24 in the B/C/S, if you could just tell us very briefly about the structure of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The JNA was a federal organisation; i.e., it covered the six republics and two autonomous provinces. There was only one JNA for the whole of the SFRY armed forces. For the -- for the SFRY, I apologise. The JNA consisted of branches, ground forces, air force and air defence and navy, and these branches would consist of arms. For example, in the ground forces you would have infantry, artillery, armour, and so on. It would also be services like logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we need to go into any more detail now, but is it correct that at pages 28 to 34 of the report the Trial Chamber could find more details on this particular subject, the structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then continuing, looking at page 7 of your report, which is page 25 in the B/C/S, please briefly describe the structure of the Territorial Defence, or TO.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Territorial Defence, or TO, was organised on the republican level and on the level of autonomous provinces. So each of the six republics, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia, and the two autonomous provinces Vojvodina and Kosovo, would have its own TO. TO was, according to the regulations I consulted, it was called the broadest form of armed resistance. The TO were, of course, part of the SFRY armed forces; i.e., subordinated to the main -- to the same body as the JNA, but they had also some responsibilities towards their own republican or autonomous province's authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here again, we don't need to go into further detail, but if you could confirm that at pages 35 to 38 - that's 53 to 57 in B/C/S - there's more detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is, actually, one minor thing that I see there. Could you mention the difference between manoeuvre TO units and local TO units, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. According to the doctrinal documents of the SFRY armed forces I consulted, there were two types of TO units. First of all, there were the local or Territorial Defence -- Territorial Defence units, which were units that were locally recruited, for example, on the basis of a municipality, and they would stay -- they would stay in that area. These were mainly smaller units which would be used to protect certain vital facilities - radio stations, production plants, and so on - that would patrol the area, but they would rarely operate with JNA units on the first lines. The second type of Territorial Defence units were the so -- were the manoeuvre or mobile Territorial Defence units, and they are explained on page 37. These are Territorial Defence units of bigger size, and according to doctrine, they could operate in coordination with the JNA already on the first lines. That's basically what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? Were there police forces on the municipalities over and above the territorial groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, police forces were not part of the SFRY armed forces. So of course there were -- there was police, and as I have explained in the beginning of the report, and I think that's on pages -- on page 11, there is paragraph on the police. There were certain circumstances during which police could participate in combat operations, and then the police would, according to the doctrine, be subordinated to the officer in command of the military operations, which makes sense, but that would most of the times be, in most scenarios for military operation or combat operations, that would be a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. All I wanted to know and understand was that these TOs didn't do policework. They were part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the doctrine de jure, they were not involved in policework, Your Honours, but even of course patrolling the area, for example, what was called a recently liberated area -- if terrain is captured from the enemy, then the territory is called liberated -- the TO could be used for that because there would not be any police force. And there could be tasks in the framework of law and order, but again that's very theoretical, and I think when we discuss SAO Krajina and RSK TO, then we'll see how the de facto situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You in part anticipated some of my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, one -- yet another category that's mentioned in your report and also in your Milosevic testimony is volunteers. Now, just briefly, could you summarise what's meant by the word "volunteers" and how if at all that's different from paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Volunteers, Your Honours, were defined in the -- the 1982 All People's Defence Law, and according to the law, these were people who had no military obligations but who still decided they wanted to contribute to the armed -- to the operations or to the activities of the armed forces. One thing we didn't mention earlier, but the TO included all armed structures that were not part of the JNA, so if volunteers would join the armed forces, they would normally be included in Territorial Defence units. Now, particularly in the Milosevic case there was talk about paramilitary units or volunteer units. Without wanting -- wanting to take too much of the Court's time, paramilitary forces actually has two meanings. There can be legal paramilitary forces and illegal paramilitary forces. When you consult the military or another dictionary, legal paramilitary forces are forces which are allowed by the law or foreseen in the law which are not military but they can have a military structure or can carry out military duties. For example, in my own country we had a police called, in French, "gendarmerie" which was subordinated to the minister of defence until, I think, the middle of the '80s, and that could be, according to doctrine, called a paramilitary force. Of course the paramilitary forces we are talking about in this context are what we could call illegal paramilitary forces. We see -- and that's also discussed in the report on page 9 that in the course of 1991, and I look mainly at the events in Serbia, that certain political parties established their own what they called volunteer groups, which were not foreseen in the law but they were nevertheless allowed to participate in the operations. Some examples are listed there. Interestingly, according to the documents I reviewed, some of these groups, and the most famous ones like Arkan Tigers or people affiliated with Dragan, we've seen evidence documents that link these groups to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Republic of Serbia, not RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer that question, Your Honour, but then I think we're going to jump topics. We will discuss it later. There are examples, and I've discussed it in my report too, that, for example, an individual called Dragan Vasiljevic -- Vasiljkovic, excuse me, Dragan Vasiljkovic, also known under the nickname Captain Dragan, there is documentary evidence that links Dragan to not only the Serbian Ministry of the Interior but also links him to a training centre in Golubic - that's in the vicinity of Knin - where special forces of the police of the SAO Krajina were trained. And I -- I don't go into details for that, for Dragan, in my report, but I've just mentioned it to show the fact that he was also in the RSK, or SAO Krajina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you've now discussed the make-up of the SFRY armed forces. What was their mission prior to 1990?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The mission, Your Honours, as it was defined in the constitution and the All People's Defence Law consists of safeguarding the independence, territorial integrity, sovereignty, and social order of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to enter into a new topic. It's not such a radical change that I couldn't go right into it and take up after the break, but I notice we're getting close, I think, to -- are we close to the hour and 15 minute mark? Oh, no. We started late today. My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the next issue that's addressed in your report is command and control. Now, this begins at page 12 of the English, page 31 of the B/C/S. There you quote from Article 96 of a 1982 law. Could you please tell the Chamber the significance of that article.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, that article is not the most significant one. It only explains that, well, the competent federal bodies carry out command and control over the armed forces, and it's only further on in the 1982 All People's Defence Law that these bodies are defined - and this is also discussed in the report - as well as certain principles of command and control are elaborated upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have it handy, could you -- you mentioned some other articles further on. Which are the articles that you find of most significance there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Key article is explained on page 13 of the English version. It's Article 313 of the 1974 SFRY constitution, which states that the Presidency, the SFRY Presidency, is the supreme body in charge of administration and command of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, both in war and in peacetime. And of course, based on the constitution, the All People's Defence Law then specifies certain aspects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 13, if you turn there, please, you mention three levels of command and control. Could you please briefly tell what those are.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Like in any military, there are three levels of command and control; strategic level, operational level, and tactical level. For the SFRY armed forces was concerned, the strategic level consisted of what -- a body that was called the Supreme Command. I can explain it now, if -- in brief terms, if you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you can just go ahead with the three levels and then we'll come back.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay. The second level was the operational level, which corresponded with the level of military districts and corps; and below that was the tactical level, which covers all military units below the corps level formation, so it's from division, brigade, regiment, battalion, and further downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next few pages discuss various bodies within the SFRY. I'd intended to skip over that in court. It's there for your reference, but please intervene if you'd like him to give more details about the Supreme Council or any other entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if you could then turn to page 21, which is page 40 in the B/C/S version. There you deal specifically with command and control over the JNA and the TO, and you quote from a 1990 JNA regulation. What's the significance of that passage?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the significance of the passage is that it provides a definition of command and control, highlighting the main aspects of it, command and control within the military. I will not read the definition, but the key expressions are that command and control are conscious and organised activities of the commander. So it doesn't happen by coincidence that he issues an order, and of course he does it in an organised way, whereby he engages and unifies both his, if I could call it like that, human resources as well as materiel resources to implement the orders or the goal he has received in the most effective way. The second part of the definition highlights a number of aspects of command and control. Issuing an order requires, of course, that first of all you have prepared the order. You have also looked at the planning issues, and most importantly, there need to be information flows, which is highlighted -- discussed at the end. The commander needs to know the situation of his subordinate units, and of course also he needs to be in a position to report to his superiors on the status of implementation of the orders he as a commander has received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this regulation tell us about the relationship between the JNA and the Territorial Defence in terms of command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: According to the 1990 corps regulation, when JNA and TO are engaged together in military operations, the JNA officer, the most senior JNA officer will be in command of both forces, both components.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your executive summary and then elsewhere in your report, you refer to the principles of unity of command and single authority. Could you please explain both of those principles.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: These principles, Your Honour, they come from Article 112 of the 1982 All People's Defence Law, but they actually apply to any armed force. The first principle of singleness, as it is called in the definition, means that there is only one commander. If you have two commanders issuing orders at the same time to the same people, then there is a risk for chaos. So there can only be one commander and only one senior officer who receives the reports. The second principle, unity of command, is -- actually concerns what is called the coherence. It means that there needs to be coherence between the orders of the most superior command level and the orders of the lowest level. I can give an example: If the SFRY Presidency or if a Presidency that -- states that we have to defend the country against a threat from the east, it means that there will -- that the troops on the lowest level, the platoon level, will know that they have to defend themselves or defend the country against the threat from the east and not one from the south, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. And then there is a third principle, which is the principle of the obligation to implement decisions and orders, which I believe is also quite straightforward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And again we have to make an effort to go slow. I know it's hard, but we have to keep trying. On pages 22 and 23 of the report - this is page 42 of the B/C/S - you address command and control of the TO specifically, and you quote from articles 95 and 115 of this 1982 law. What do those provisions tell us about command and control of the TO before the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: They address both command and control within the TO forces only, as well always the fact that the TO forces in the command and control over the TO forces; i.e., that the TO forces, Territorial Defence, are subordinated to the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next subject which I'd like to touch on is the interaction between the JNA and the TO, again prior to 1990. Could you summarise what that relationship was like in terms of command structure or cooperation between the JNA and the TO.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, we touched upon that earlier. By applying the principles of command and control, singleness, unity of command, and also the obligation to implement decisions, it meant that if JNA and TO would be engaged together in military operations, there would only be one commander. For most scenarios for military operations, it would be the JNA officer who would be in command. However, there were also scenarios where a TO commander could be in command. For example, the situation that was described as temporary occupation of the territory. It means that the SFRY armed forces are on the defence, an enemy force has invaded the country and temporarily occupies certain sections of the territory. Then a TO commander could be in command, which makes sense because he knows the local territory better than the JNA as the JNA was trained to fight on the first lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer focused mostly on operations. Just so we have the full picture, what about issues like equipment and training? How were those handled?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because the TOs were republican structures, it were the republics who were responsible for training and equipping and financing their TOs, and the commander of the republican TO was accountable to the president of the republic; i.e., the component republic, for these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In a joint operation between the TO and the JNA, how would the funding be arranged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would expect that funding -- I mean, of course -- if it means the funding in order to be able to operate, that would have been sorted out before. The republics were responsible for training and financing the TO, so it was -- it were the republics who were responsible for then the state of readiness of that TO. Now, a second aspects, of course, is doing operations. Soldiers need to be paid. And there we see from documents we have reviewed for the structure known as the SAO Krajina TO that there were certain complaints from members of that TO because they said, "We are not paid." But that -- those are, let's say, very de facto situations and maybe we can elaborate on that later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your report you say that over time there was an effort to centralise control of the TO. Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. We see that in 1998 a restructuring plan called Jedinstvo, or unity, which had been actually adopted in 1986, is implemented, and then it has a number of implications for the structure of the JNA but also for command and control over the TO. Basically, it meant that whereas initially the TO was subordinated to the SFRY Presidency so that the chain of commands would only join at the level of the Presidency, after Jedinstvo, the chain of command would join at the local level, at the level of the military districts, and that was most obvious via the order which renamed the chief of General Staff of the JNA into the chief of General Staff of the SFRY armed forces. Now, in the report - this is discussed on the pages 25 through to 26 - the backgrounds of this decision are discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned an order, and I'm just trying to make sure that I'm looking at the right one. Is that the 14th May 1990 order, or is that a different one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was discussing a different order, but the 14th of May, 1990, order, which is mentioned on page 26 of the English version, is actually part of this -- this -- this move to acquire what I could consider greater control over the republican TOs. I've quoted from a book by the then federal secretary for all people's defence, General Kadijevic, as well as an expert report by a Colonel Radinovic, which has been filed here in another case, but Radinovic himself was involved in Jedinstvo , where both senior officers actually explain that they were convinced that the republics, in particular Slovenia and Croatia, were planning to develop their TOs into republican armed forces, and a number of senior officers in the JNA, or you could consider them pro-Yugoslav officers, they wanted to prevent that, and Jedinstvo is one aspect. You lower the subordination level. The 14th of May, 1990, order is a second aspect. By that order, the weapons of the Territorial Defence were stored in warehouses all over Yugoslavia, in warehouses under the control of these republics, by these orders these weapons had to be transferred from TO, let's say controlled facilities, to facilities under JNA control which, by people in the republics, was seen as like disarmament of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move forward a little bit, we'll look at pages 39 to 41 of your report. This is page 56 to 59 in B/C/S. Here you talk about operational groups, or OG, and tactical groups, TGs. Could you please explain what those were and how they functioned in the context of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. SFRY doctrine foresaw the establishment of operational groups, also known as OGs, and tactical groups, TGs, in order to apply the earlier mentioned principles of command and control during operations. Based on the fact that we have two components, JNA and TO, they may have exercised together and trained together, but when military operations are being conducted, it could well be that units of -- different parent units, for example, brigades from different JNA corps, would cooperate together with TO units who had no previous experience of operating together, and therefore operational groups on almost your corps level, between corps and division level, and tactical groups, which had the size more or less of a brigade, were established. These were temporary formations unifying JNA and TO with one command which were established for specific operations in specific areas. One regulation says that they were remained -- that they were an exception and that they were only established when certain circumstances forced the creation of such units. For example, difficult terrain. If very mountainous terrain exists which would make it difficult for units to communicate with each other, then it could be facilitated by having a joint command -- joint is not the best word in this context, but a common command over these units, which could then solve these problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you touched on the issue of command. How did command work in an operational group or a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It worked according to the previously mentioned principles; i.e., that the command of the operational group or the tactical group, he issues the orders to all components of the operational group; so JNA and TO. There are also examples discussed in the third section of the report where in some areas elements of the police of the SAO or -- for the SAO Krajina are involved and then they are also mentioned in the orders of the commander of the operational group or the commander of the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on then just a couple more topics in section 1. At pages 41 to 50 of the report - this is 59 to 69, I believe, in the B/C/S - the report -- well, you addressed the laws of war and international humanitarian law. I don't want to spend a lot of court time on this, but briefly, what was the position of the SFRY armed forces towards such law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these -- these issues were discussed in the 1988 regulations on the application of the international laws of war in the SFRY armed forces - so it applied to both JNA and TO - and basically the ideas and principles that I explained in these regulations correspond with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient for our purposes now. And then at pages 50 to 56, or 69 to 75 in the B/C/S, you addressed the investigation and prosecution of violations of the law of armed conflict. We won't cover this in detail but I would just direct your attention to the first sentence of this section on page 50 and ask you who in the armed forces of the SFRY had an obligation to report violations of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the regulations, and in particular the 1988 regulation I mentioned before, each SFRY armed forces officer was obliged to report violations of the laws of war. In addition to that, the military police and organs or officers called security organs had additional responsibilities in that field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, that's -- yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could a junior officer report a violation of a law of war by a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the regulations, Your Honour, indeed he had -- he could -- it was not only that he could but he had to. And maybe he would in this case be reluctant to -- if his commander had been involved, he would be reluctant to do it via his commander, but he could contact military police or security organs and then indeed fulfil his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a convenient place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court will adjourn. We will reconvene at quarter past four. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the interpreters have pleaded with me over the break to ask you to go more slowly, and for me also. I think, on their advice, one way that may help us do it is to focus on the pauses between question and answer. So after I ask a question, wait a moment before you get started and that will help everybody keep up. Mr. Theunens, we finished discussing section 1 of your report. Section 2 addresses the legislative framework applicable to defence matters in the Republic of Serbia. Now, if you could, just very briefly explain the relevance of that section to this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, section 2, which covers armed force of the Republic of Serbia, was included because on the 1st of August, 1991, a decision was taken in the entity known as the SAO Krajina to adopt the defence law of the Republic of Serbia as the defence law of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was that effective, that situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This situation was effective until November 1991, when the SAO Krajina adopted its own law of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those are all the questions I have on section 2 of the report. So we'll move now straight ahead into section 3. This section starts at page 66 in the English, and page 85 in the B/C/S. Mr. Theunens, so far we've been discussing the situation prior to about 1990. Now, obviously after 1990 there were important events in the political landscape which will be addressed by other witnesses in the case. What I'd like to ask you about is the impact of those political events on military matters. Earlier you explained the mission of the SFRY armed forces prior to 1990, and that included the JNA. Now, turning now to the years 1990, 1991, 1992, did your analysis reveal any change in their law? Of the JNA, I'm focussed on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the documents I reviewed, and they included both books by senior and political and military authorities from that time in the SFRY, as well as military orders, it is obvious that at the latest in summer 1991, and we could be more specific by mentioning September 1991, that there is a change in the mission of the JNA, and that this mission changes into what is called by these -- by these documents and sources I quoted as protecting and liberating the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some specific questions about the basis for this conclusion as set forth in your report. First, who was Veljko Kadijevic? I think you mentioned him earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, army general Veljko Kadijevic was known as the federal secretary for people's defence, which could be compared to a minister of defence even though he had a clear -- he played a clear role in the command and control of the SFRY armed forces. If you want, Your Honour, I can explain the concepts of Supreme Command in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the legislation discussed in part 1 of the report, when a state of emergency or a state of war or a state of -- imminent state of war would be declared, then the SFRY Presidency would become the Supreme Command. The federal secretary for people's defence would then become the chief of staff of the staff of the Supreme Command, whereby the staff of the Supreme Command is -- consists of the Federal Secretariat; i.e., the -- call it the Ministry of Defence, but it was called Federal Secretariat of People's Defence. And that was the role that General Kadijevic fulfilled during the crisis or the conflict in Croatia until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And two follow-up questions to that. First, to be clear, we're still talking about the SFRY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And second, in your report, I believe you used an abbreviation, SSNO. Could you just tell us what that abbreviation is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, SSNO is the B/C/S acronym for Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, or some people translate the N, "Narodna," as National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens with the assistance of the court officer, I'm going to ask you to look at a document. These are the published memoirs of Mr. Kadijevic, entitled "My view of the break-up." The 65 ter number is 1370, and the B/C/S ERN, the original ERN, is 00359426. And while that's being pulled up on the screen, Mr. Theunens, could you just summarise what that document tells us. Tell us the importance of that document.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this book is called "My view of the break-up," in English, and it was written by Veljko Kadijevic in 1993. From my activities here at the OTP, at Office of the Prosecutor, including interviewing witnesses, it is clear that Veljko Kadijevic had access to certain JNA archives in order to compile this book. In his book he gives a personal account of how not only SFRY dissolved but also how the mission of the SFRY armed forces, and specifically the JNA, developed over time. And I must say he does it in a very methodical, military way, distinguishing phases and stages, mentioning names and locations and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, or according to your report, Kadijevic refers to two stages of the conflict. Could you explain those two stages, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Actually, the expression Kadijevic uses is "phases." He -- Kadijevic makes a distinction between a first phase, which according to him starts with the first attacks on Serbs in Croatia and ends in summer 1991. The second phase, according to Kadijevic, starts end of summer 1991 and lasts until the adoption of the Vance Peace Plan. In the second phase, Kadijevic distinguishes two stages; a first stage which lasts more or less until, if I'm not wrong, the end of September. And the second stage then covers the period end of September to adoption of the Vance Plan, which is 2nd of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happens during that -- during those two stages of the second phase?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, for the purpose of this report the second phase is the most relevant, because according to what Kadijevic writes, the mission of the JNA, he uses the expression "radically," "radically changes," and the JNA focuses on -- actually, on three things: First of all, what he calls liberating and protecting the Serbs; secondly, according to Kadijevic, to remove Croatian forces from areas considered Serb; and thirdly, withdrawing the JNA from besieged barracks -- from the barracks and garrisons that were besieged in certain parts of Croatia. If you allow, Your Honours, in the report, there are two maps covering the second phase. These maps are not included in Kadijevic's book, but are based on my interpretation of what is described in the book for these two stages of the second phase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mention, please, the page numbers of those maps, in English.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The first map is mentioned -- or is included on page 75 of the report. And in the footnote, you can find back the pages of the English version of Kadijevic's book on which -- or whereon this map is based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second map, I believe, is on page 76; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you please explain what's depicted in this map on page 76. And by the way, that's page 95 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Kadijevic states that the second stage of the second phase involved the following operations, and they are described on the top of page 76. First of all, he says that in close coordination with what he calls Serb insurgents, all Serb regions in Croatia, except for part of Western Slavonia, were liberated. And that's basically where the map refers to. Now, the map, as I put it there, reflects the situation as it was when the Vance Plan was adopted; i.e. - I think we will speak about it later - a number of UN protected areas were defined, and the red zones correspond with the territories covered by these UNPAs, except for Western Slavonia where the UNPA went much further to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt. You're referring to red zones. Now, your map at page 76 is a photocopy. Is it possible, Mr. Black, that this map is in this bunch that you gave; and if so, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It should follow the same numbering, so it should say page 76 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we'll return to the issues about the Vance Plan and the UNPAs in a moment, but I don't know, do you still have the maps booklet there by you? I'd ask you to turn to map 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if you could just look there at map 7 and tell me how it compares to what's shown at page 76 of your report just generally.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the zones I represented in red on the map on page 76 of my report corresponds with the areas delineated by the red lines on map number 7, taking into account that a different projection system -- or different projection has been used for the map on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just so the record's clear, Your Honour, that's page 7 -- or map 7 of Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we won't go through this entire book, of course, but could you indicate to the Trial Chamber the pages or parts of this book that are most relevant to what you've just told us. This is in Kadijevic's book.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In the -- I will start with the B/C/S version. It is between the ERNs 00359489 and 00359499. And in the English version this corresponds with pages 00362685, 2686, 2697, 2704 until 2710, and the page 00362713.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is, I think, one of the two or three longest documents. I don't propose to go through all of those pages. At this time, I'd move that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be easiest if the entire book is admitted, but if -- just the relevant pages is certainly fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the book that is on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What exhibit number shall we give it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 24, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, at pages 77 to 80 of your report, you reduce -- you reproduce parts of two documents, and I'm going to ask you questions about both of them. This is pages 96 to 99 of the B/C/S. First, there's a statement -- another statement by Kadijevic. And this is 65 ter number 1850, for the court officer. The B/C/S ERN is 04620065 to 0066. If that could be put on the E-court, please. Mr. Theunens, you also have a hard copy of that in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, maybe I can go ahead and give you the question as it's being brought up on E-court. What does this statement tell us about the JNA position by October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honours, I would like to mention that this here is a statement, a contemporaneous statement; i.e., a statement made by Kadijevic on the 3rd of October, 1991, which was published in the Bulletin, or "Bilten" in B/C/S, of the information service of the SSNO. So it was a public information publication that was mainly intended for the international media, and that explains -- and international press. That explains why it is in French. In this statement, Kadijevic basically mentions two important points: First of all, he criticises the Supreme Command, or more specifically the Croatian members of the Supreme Command. And also, he clearly puts on paper the new mission of the JNA; i.e., to protect the Serbian population. He uses expressions like "genocide," "neo-Nazism," and "Ustasha forces," which is quite significant when looking at the level at which this statement is issued. It's the highest military level, and it's used for public consumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that it's clear, when you say he uses expressions like "genocide" and "neo-Nazism" and "Ustasha," please clarify the context in which he uses them. What does he say with those expressions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Basically -- I apologise for the lack of pause. Kadijevic describes the situation as he sees it in Croatia, and he, for example, mentions - and I'm reading from the document - that: "There is repetition of genocide against the Serb people." In another paragraph he mentions: "What is in force in the Republic of Croatia is neo-Nazism." And he says that: "Neo-Nazism is the most serious threat to the Serbian people in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you, what is he referring to there in terms of neo-Nazism, and also the expression "Ustasha"? What is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: He -- Kadijevic makes the link to the events of the Second World War during which, in 1941, an entity known as the NDH, the Croatian Independent State, was installed, which -- I'm not an historian, but based on the documents I read, could be considered a puppet state of or the axis of Nazi Germany, and indeed then there were serious crimes against Serbs living in Croatia committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does "Ustasha" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, "Ustasha" was -- based on what I've seen, was first used in 1929.
